book.title: In the Realm of Hungry Ghosts
book.author: Gabor Maté

confidence_note: The book pairs Rat Park with the Vietnam data in chapter 12 (two tables of contents, chapter summaries), but the book text was not read; experiment details come from Alexander's papers as summarised by Wikipedia. Old text dropped: oxytocin and dopamine mechanism, the "antidote is connection" line (Johann Hari's phrase), clinical observations, "until death".
facts: Chapter 12, "From Vietnam to Rat Park", sets Bruce Alexander's rat experiments beside the Vietnam data to argue that addiction's roots are environmental.
Alexander and colleagues at Simon Fraser University published the work between 1978 and 1981.

Rat Park was an enclosure with 200 times the floor area of a standard lab cage, holding 16 to 20 rats of both sexes with food, balls, wheels and room to mate. Control rats lived alone in small metal cages.
Each rat had two drop dispensers: sweetened morphine solution and plain tap water. The sweetener was meant to cover morphine's bitter taste.
Park rats mostly chose plain water. In one condition caged males drank up to 19 times more morphine than Park males.
Rats kept 57 days on morphine only, then given a choice in Rat Park, chose plain water and showed only minor withdrawal signs.
Caveats: Bruce Petrie (1996), a former student of Alexander, could not replicate it; critics cite small samples, bitter oral morphine, uneven measurement and equipment failures.
Design: four groups of eight rats (32), caged or in the park from weaning (day 22) to day 80, two groups swapped at day 65; females sampled morphine more than males.
Johann Hari's 2015 TED talk popularized the study; researchers say the media oversold it as a paradigm shift.
scene_details: Two drop dispensers per rat, one morphine and one water
A wire-and-metal cage for one rat beside an enclosure 200 times larger with wheels and balls
Rats moved after 57 days of forced morphine choosing water
tension: The same drug in the same bottle was drunk very differently depending on where the rat lived.
opening_idea: Start with the two dispensers and the two ways of housing the rats.

lessons.idea: Before blaming a trait, change one condition and see whether the behaviour moves.
lessons.anchor: Same morphine, same rats, different housing, different drinking.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A teenager called lazy about homework who works fine at a library table instead of a crowded kitchen.

reflect_final: Which behaviour of yours or of someone close would you re-read if you changed where or with whom it happens?

use_cases.move: Cite the rats that drank less once housing changed and propose swapping one condition for two weeks.

use_cases.situation: A family member is blamed for a habit.
use_cases.move: Ask what the days around the habit look like and who is around.

use_cases.situation: You keep failing at something at home.
use_cases.move: Try it once in another room or place and watch what changes.

pocket_idea: The rats in the big enclosure mostly skipped the morphine: change the surroundings before blaming the appetite.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Alexander's rats chose plain water over morphine when their cage became a park.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Alexander compared lone caged rats with rats in a 200-times-larger enclosure, each offered sweet morphine or water; the park rats mostly drank water; later labs failed to repeat it.
